clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Regularized Discriminant Analysis (RDA) classifiers were trained using percentile scores from growth curves to distinguish ASD from TDC. Three classifiers were developed based on different feature sets: (1) subregional volumes only (6 features), (2) midsagittal plane features only (4 features), and (3) combined features (10 features). 10-fold cross-validation was used. Performance was evaluated using mean classification accuracy and area under the ROC curve (AUC). Group differences in percentiles were also examined using t-tests. Mahalanobis distance was calculated to summarize multivariate deviation.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Sex-specific growth curve models revealed nonlinear developmental trajectories with region-specific growth rates and earlier developmental peaks in females; classifiers trained on growth curve deviations accurately distinguished ASD from TDC (mean AUC = 0.95), demonstrating cross-scanner generalizability.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study established sex-specific GAMLSS growth curve models for 10 corpus callosum morphometric parameters in 295 typically developing children aged 1-6 years. Key findings include: (1) Nonlinear developmental patterns with the most rapid changes occurring before age 4; (2) Regional differences in growth rates, with mid-anterior and central regions showing consistently high growth rates in both sexes; (3) Significant sex differences in most metrics (p < 0.033 for all except circularity and length), with projected developmental peaks occurring earlier in females (7.5-10.5 years) than males (9-13 years); (4) When applied to an independent dataset from a different scanner (3T Philips), the models successfully identified ASD children (n=26) from TDC (n=41), with ASD showing left-skewed percentile distributions (indicating over-maturation) for mid-anterior volume, central volume, and all five global metrics; (5) Classification accuracy was high: combined features AUC=0.95, subregional volumes AUC=0.916, midsagittal features AUC=0.894; (6) ASD children showed significantly larger corpus callosum morphometrics compared to TDC for all metrics except anterior subregion volume; (7) Mahalanobis distance was significantly higher in ASD (median 42.65) versus TDC (median 9.42), indicating greater multivariate deviation; (8) The most common aberration in ASD was overlarge volume of the central subregion of the corpus callosum.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study demonstrates that sex-specific corpus callosum growth curve models can serve as a quantitative, generalizable tool for characterizing typical development and detecting atypical morphometry in neurodevelopmental disorders. The high cross-scanner classification accuracy (AUC=0.95) suggests the biological signal of atypical corpus callosum morphology in ASD is robust enough to be detected across different imaging platforms (1.5T Siemens vs 3T Philips), which is crucial for potential clinical translation. The authors suggest this approach could offer a promising method for early, objective ASD diagnosis, potentially facilitating timely intervention. The use of different scanners for model construction and validation was a deliberate design choice to stringently test real-world generalizability. However, the authors emphasize that further study of model generalizability across more diverse populations, sites, and scanners is warranted before widespread clinical deployment. The heterogeneous pattern of deviations across individuals and metrics suggests the potential for using these models to identify ASD subtypes or to stratify patients for personalized interventions.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Several limitations are acknowledged: (1) Cross-sectional design captures population-level trends rather than individual developmental trajectories; longitudinal data would better characterize individual growth patterns; (2) The TDC cohort was recruited from a clinical population (children referred for MRI due to various concerns like febrile seizures, dizziness, headache, etc., though ultimately showing no neurological abnormalities), which may introduce more variance than a community-based sample and make findings more conservative; (3) Projections of peak developmental ages extend beyond the 1-to-6-year data range and should be considered exploratory hypotheses rather than definitive findings; they serve only to contextualize sex differences observed in early childhood; (4) Limited age range (1-6 years) does not capture full developmental trajectory; broader age ranges (e.g., 1-16 years) would better characterize growth patterns across developmental stages; (5) Validation was performed at the same institution using a different scanner, but further validation in diverse populations and settings is needed; (6) The sedation protocol (used for children under 4 and some older uncooperative children) may have affected image quality or developmental variance, though this was not explicitly modeled.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study represents a focused application of normative modeling to early childhood corpus callosum development (ages 1-6 years), a relatively understudied age range. The deliberate use of different scanners for model construction (1.5T Siemens) and validation (3T Philips) is a notable methodological strength, providing strong evidence for cross-scanner generalizability. Age-specific templates (publicly available at https://osf.io/fm7cq) were used for six age groups to account for rapid developmental changes in brain size and gray-white matter contrast. The study population included children who underwent MRI for various clinical concerns (simple febrile seizures, dizziness, headache, facial/arm numbness, trauma, transient fever of unknown origin, routine physical examinations) but were ultimately included in TDC after ruling out neurological diagnoses. Sedation protocol: all children under 4 years were sedated; among children over 4, those who were cooperative were scanned while calm, but sedation (10% chloral hydrate, 50 mg/kg body weight, oral or rectal) was used for uncooperative children after psychological guidance failed. Gender determination was based on parents' self-assessment for both ASD and TDC participants. The GAMLSS models used Box-Cox t (BCT) distribution selected based on AIC and BIC comparison. Bootstrap resampling (1000 resamples) was used to estimate 95% confidence intervals for the median growth curves. The study follows WHO methodology for growth curve construction. FreeSurfer and Yuki software have been validated for pediatric corpus callosum segmentation in prior studies. Post-segmentation quality checks were performed with manual corrections using ITK-SNAP when needed. This is one of the first studies to construct detailed, sex-specific growth curves for multiple corpus callosum morphometrics in the 1-6 year age range and to demonstrate their utility in identifying ASD with high accuracy across different scanners.
